params.question: In a full-term newborn, the intracellular fluid compartment is larger than the extracellular fluid compartment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: In adults, the intracellular compartment is indeed larger than the extracellular. However, in newborns this relationship is reversed: extracellular fluid is 40–45% of body weight versus only 30–40% for intracellular fluid. This large extracellular pool is the compartment drained first by vomiting and diarrhoea, which is why young infants dehydrate so rapidly.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. In a newborn, extracellular fluid (40–45% of body weight) is actually larger than intracellular fluid (~30–40%). This is the opposite of the adult pattern, where ICF (~40%) exceeds ECF (20–25%). The intracellular compartment gradually catches up as muscle mass develops through childhood.

params.question: A 2-year-old boy with acute diarrhoea is brought to a health centre. He is restless, has sunken eyes, drinks water eagerly, and his skin pinch goes back slowly. Under the IMNCI classification, what is his dehydration category and correct management?

answers.text: No dehydration — Plan A: extra home fluids and continued feeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A child with 'no dehydration' would be alert and well, with no sunken eyes, a moist mouth, and a skin pinch that snaps back immediately. This child has multiple abnormal signs that indicate a higher category.

answers.text: Some dehydration — Plan B: supervised oral rehydration at the health facility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Two or more signs — restlessness, sunken eyes, eager thirst, and a slow skin pinch — together classify as 'some dehydration' under IMNCI (5–9% body weight loss). Plan B involves supervised oral rehydration at a health facility.

answers.text: Severe dehydration — Plan C: immediate intravenous fluids and hospitalisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severe dehydration requires more alarming signs such as drowsiness or inability to drink, very sunken eyes, or a very slow skin pinch. This child is restless (not drowsy) and drinking eagerly, which points to 'some dehydration'.

answers.text: Moderate dehydration — Plan B: intravenous normal saline at 20 mL/kg bolus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 'Moderate dehydration' is not a category in the IMNCI framework. IMNCI classifies dehydration into three groups only: no dehydration, some dehydration, and severe dehydration. Plan B uses oral rehydration, not intravenous fluids.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the IMNCI classification: restlessness, sunken eyes, eager thirst, and slow skin pinch together indicate 'some dehydration' (5–9% loss), managed with Plan B (supervised oral rehydration at a health facility).

Well done. Recognising restlessness, sunken eyes, eager thirst, and slow skin pinch as 'some dehydration' directs you to Plan B — supervised oral rehydration at a health facility, not home management or IV fluids.

params.question: A child develops seizures and reduced consciousness after receiving a large volume of hypotonic intravenous fluid over 4 hours. Serum sodium is 125 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the neurological symptoms?

answers.text: Rapid brain cell shrinkage as water moves out of neurons due to high extracellular osmolality

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cell shrinkage occurs in hypernatraemia, where elevated extracellular sodium draws water out of cells. In this child, sodium is low, so the osmotic gradient drives water in the opposite direction — into the cells.

answers.text: Cerebral oedema from water shifting into brain cells down the osmotic gradient created by the acute fall in extracellular sodium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Acute hyponatraemia lowers extracellular osmolality, driving water into brain cells and causing cerebral oedema. The rapid onset (4 hours) is especially dangerous because the brain has had no time to activate compensatory mechanisms such as extruding intracellular osmoles.

answers.text: Depolarisation of neuronal membranes from excess extracellular potassium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Membrane depolarisation from excess extracellular potassium produces ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS) and ascending paralysis — the pattern of hyperkalaemia, not hyponatraemia.

answers.text: Osmotic demyelination of brainstem pathways caused by the rapid fall in sodium concentration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Osmotic demyelination syndrome results from overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia, not from the hyponatraemia itself. It is a complication of treatment, not of the primary electrolyte disturbance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key mechanism is osmotic water movement. When extracellular sodium drops acutely, water moves INTO brain cells (not out), producing cerebral oedema. Osmotic demyelination, by contrast, is a complication of too-rapid correction, not of the hyponatraemia itself.

Excellent. Acute hyponatraemia causes osmotic water movement into brain cells, producing cerebral oedema. The speed of the fall — just 4 hours here — makes this far more dangerous than the same sodium level reached gradually.

params.question: A 5-year-old child has serum sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, and metabolic alkalosis. Urine sodium is below 10 mmol/L. Which clinical scenario is most consistent with this combination of findings?

answers.text: Renal tubular acidosis causing renal sodium and potassium wasting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal tubular acidosis produces metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. It also causes renal sodium wasting, so urine sodium would be above 20 mmol/L — the opposite of what is seen here.

In SIADH, the kidneys do not conserve sodium — urine sodium is typically above 20 mmol/L. The low urine sodium (<10) here indicates the kidneys are holding onto sodium tightly, pointing to losses from outside the kidney.

answers.text: Persistent vomiting causing extrarenal sodium and potassium losses with secondary aldosterone activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Persistent vomiting causes loss of hydrochloric acid (producing metabolic alkalosis) along with sodium and potassium from the gastrointestinal tract. The kidney responds by avidly retaining sodium (urine Na <10). Low potassium with metabolic alkalosis is a classic pattern of extrarenal losses.

answers.text: Adrenal insufficiency with combined mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adrenal insufficiency causes hyperkalaemia (not hypokalaemia), because aldosterone — which drives renal potassium excretion — is deficient. It also produces metabolic acidosis, not the metabolic alkalosis seen here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Read the electrolytes together: low sodium + low potassium + metabolic alkalosis + urine Na <10 indicates extrarenal losses (e.g. vomiting). The low urine sodium tells you the kidneys are conserving sodium, ruling out renal causes like SIADH or renal tubular acidosis.

Excellent analysis. Reading the electrolytes together — low sodium, low potassium, metabolic alkalosis, urine sodium <10 — points to extrarenal losses such as persistent vomiting, with the kidney appropriately conserving sodium.

params.question: A child with acute renal failure has a serum potassium of 7.2 mmol/L. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS complex. What is the most important first step in management?

answers.text: Administer oral sodium polystyrene sulphonate to remove potassium from the body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral resins such as sodium polystyrene sulphonate do remove total body potassium over time, but their onset is far too slow for a child with ECG changes indicating imminent dangerous arrhythmia. The heart must be stabilised first.

answers.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Calcium gluconate does not lower potassium itself, but it stabilises the cardiac cell membrane against the effects of hyperkalaemia, buying time for other treatments (insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, furosemide) to shift or remove potassium.

answers.text: Give intravenous insulin with dextrose to shift potassium into cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Insulin with dextrose effectively shifts potassium into cells, but it is the second step. When ECG changes are present, the immediate priority is protecting the heart with intravenous calcium gluconate before deploying potassium-lowering agents.

answers.text: Restrict dietary potassium and stop all potassium-containing intravenous fluids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Removing potassium sources is appropriate for mild hyperkalaemia without ECG changes. With peaked T waves and a widening QRS, dietary restriction alone is dangerously insufficient — the myocardium needs immediate pharmacological stabilisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: When ECG changes are present in hyperkalaemia, the first priority is cardiac protection with intravenous calcium gluconate. It does not lower potassium itself, but it stabilises the heart while insulin–dextrose and other agents take effect.
Well done. In severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is always the first step — it stabilises the myocardium while you deploy treatments that actually lower potassium levels.
